utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-11-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: For the Prosecution, Mr. Alex Whiting and my name is Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. KASTRATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For -- the Defence team consists of myself, Strahinja Kastratovic, and my assistant Marko Kastratovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. May I attend to the distinguished representatives from the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Would you please introduce yourselves and your colleague to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Savo Markovic, Federal Minister of Justice, and I will present the guarantees of the federal government and the government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Dusan Vukasinovic, first counsellor of the Yugoslav embassy in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This Trial Chamber is very grateful for your appearance on such short notice. We appreciate your coming to The Hague with your delegation, which indicates the willingness of the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to cooperate with the Tribunal. We may ask you to address the Chamber and ask you some questions at a later stage. Mr. Martic, are you hearing the proceedings in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. I can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Today's hearing will be divided into two sittings. The first is the provisional release hearing. The second is the Status Conference. Between the two, we will have a very short break. In the Order scheduling a hearing on the motion for provisional release under Status Conference rendered by this Trial Chamber on 9 September, 2002, the Chamber considered itself seized of the motion for provisional release filed by the former counsel Knoops on the July 9th, 2002, and after request for provisional release until the beginning of the trial filed by the accused on July 10th, 2002. This Trial Chamber also received the reply of the Prosecutor dated July 18th, 2002, and a guarantee of the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the government of Serbia. The provisional release hearing will, therefore, be conducted on the basis of these provisions. Here is the full bench of the Trial Chamber. Sitting on my right is Honourable Judge El Mahdi, and sitting on my left is Honourable Judge Orie. My name is Liu, the presiding Judge of this Trial Chamber. Since the Defence counsel applied for the provisional release of Mr. Martic, I would like to turn to Mr. Kastratovic first. Would you, please, outline the main points in your request very briefly and add anything that you feel that is new. Mr. Kastratovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. KASTRATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for this opportunity to speak. At the outset, I would like to say that you don't have my appeals in this case. You have the appeal by Mr. Knoops, the lawyer from Amsterdam, which was written rather formally and does not include certain significant circumstances which should have been included. Formally speaking, only because Mr. Knoops was never accepted by Mr. Martic, the accused in this case, as his own counsel. Figuratively speaking, the dispute between the Prosecutor's office and the accused lasted for two months, during which time Mr. Martic was deprived of Defence counsel. He is a sick man, a man in detention, and as a patient has the right to choose the surgeon who will operate on him. The accused person has the right to choose his own counsel. Thanks, however, to the decision of this Trial Chamber, I am here again as his Defence counsel. At the outset, you asked me to be brief. I would like, however, to ask you for a certain amount of patience, although I will be using your time sparingly. Since you do not have in front of you my appeal, however, I need to elaborate in greater detail about the case of my client. You know that his indictment was raised in 1995 and became effective only the 21st of September this year. He has been in detention for four months now. In one of the following stages, we will discuss the events that took place during those four months. I have to stress, however, whichever way we look at it, the Court bases its decisions exclusively on law. However, there is always a political side to things, and even though I will be abusing my rights to a certain extent, I must point this fact out. Mr. Martic was a leader of a nation which no longer exists in Croatia. Starting from 1991 when the first 182 villages were evacuated from Western Slovenia and then on the 1st and 2nd of May of 1995, in the so-called military operation, the remaining 30.000 people were driven out from that part of Croatia, which was followed by the notorious date of the 5th of August, 1995, when in the Knin Krajina, the remaining 250 to 300.000 Serbs were expelled from Croatia. I do have to remind you of this at this point, although this topic will be much discussed, I'm certain, in the months that follow. Let me also remind you that once upon a time, there was about a million Serbs in Croatia. Nowadays there are no more than 100 to 120.000. The rest were expelled in a brutal operation of ethnic cleansing. Those were the Serbs who had lived in Croatia for many hundreds of years. Has anyone from -- has anyone yet answered before this Court for the expelling of Serbs from Croatia? Many thousands of people were driven out of Croatia and now live in Serbia, Montenegro, and elsewhere. Do we have here before this court any of the commanders who commanded this operation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kastratovic, I have to remind you that today is a hearing of the provisional release of your client; we are not discussing about potential issues of this case, and we will not discuss about the previous counsel, the counsel assigned by this Trial Chamber. I hope you could concentrate on the reason why you applied for the provisional release of your client. There are plenty of opportunities in the future for you to address to this Court about the substantial matters of this case. We'll give you the opportunity at a later stage. Please concentrate on the very issue of today's hearing, that is, the provisional release of your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. KASTRATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you allow me to continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. KASTRATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand this warning, but it seems to me that I have been trying to paint a picture of an injustice, precisely the injustice which brought my client here to the dock. This is the reason for this little speech of mine. I'm not now speaking to the merits of our case. This is just something that I would like the Honourable Trial Chamber to bear in mind when deciding about my client's case. As for other reasons of a more personal nature, I would like to remind you, Your Honours, that my client uttered a sentence which I second. From the very beginning, I have had a great trust in this Tribunal. My client has trust in this Tribunal from the day when government adopted the law on cooperation with it. Many people have appeared with this Tribunal, backed by guarantees from my government, which you will later deliberate upon. I have one misgiving, however, namely that you are not really giving great credit to my country's willingness to cooperate with the Tribunal. It seems to me that the experience that my government and my people have of cooperation with this Tribunal and with the Office of the Prosecutor are pending the credibility in that -- of that cooperation. Certain people have already been granted provisional release on grounds of sickness and other grounds and have been returned -- and have returned to their homeland. During the military operation, when 300.000 Serbs were driven out of Croatia, my client moved to Serbia, became a citizen of Serbia, of Croatia, and was never involved in politics again. That means that from 1995, he has partaken of the same misfortune, he has shared the same suffering that his people have undergone. But from that day onwards, he no longer took part in the civil war. He lost whatever he had together with his people, and he was only interested in seeing what the international community would do to prevent this misfortune. He is a permanent resident of Yugoslavia. He has a Yugoslav passport. His family resides there. His son is a student of law. Another son is a student of political sciences. His spouse lives there. And he has absolutely no reason to violate the guarantees provided by his government. Let me now turn to another point, special guarantees and special circumstances, that he would report to a police station in Vrnjacka Banja regularly, once in 30 days, or perhaps even in shorter intervals and that he would report any change of address if he moves to Belgrade. I would like to abstain from suggesting that you release my client, Milan Martic, the very moment when I provide you with abundant medical certificates confirming that my client is seriously ill. He has serious problems with sugar in his blood, the levels of which are extremely unstable and seriously endanger his health. There is another thing that my client would like to notify to the Office of the Prosecutor through this Trial Chamber. If my learned friends from the Prosecution would agree to it in -- pursuant to Rule 71, either here in The Hague or in Belgrade, this accused can grant an interview to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor either here or in Belgrade depending on the agreement reached between us and the decision of this Honourable Trial Chamber. I think I have explained clearly in my written submission that there is no reason why my client should not be granted provisional release. He will refrain from any public statement for the entire duration of these proceedings. He will have full respect for this process, including the political process and the fact-finding process. And I should like to say that although I have taken up some more of your time, I hope that I have convinced you of my client's sincerity. My colleague Mr. Knoops was not in a position to present these additional reasons simply because he had no contact with my client. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. May we hear the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name, again, is Alex Whiting. I will be addressing this part of the hearing today. And keeping in mind the Court's request that we be brief and try to bring to the Court's attention any new matters which may be relevant since our filing of 18 July. Our first point is that the surrender -- that the accused's surrender in this case was not a voluntary surrender. The accused -- as we argued in our submission, the accused surrendered in this case only when he had no other choice, when he was, in fact, compelled by the law on cooperation that was passed in Serbia and was facing immediate arrest. The accused himself, as we attached to our submission, stated that -- stated that just before surrendering he thought he would never be forced to surrender, that he hoped that Serbia would never extradite fugitives is to the Tribunal, that he believed that the new law on cooperation was illegal and inconsistent with the constitution and that he only surrendered, in his words, because he had no other choice. In addition, a point that I don't think was sufficiently made in our response, was the law on cooperation included another provision which stated that had if fugitives surrendered immediately before arrest, they would then obtain by law the guarantees from Serbia and from the federal -- the federal government. Therefore, the accused obviously made a calculation when the law was passed that he was facing immediate arrest and also if he surrendered before he was arrested he would obtain those guarantees and thereby enhance his chance of obtaining release. When weighed against seven years of refusing to surrender and define an indictment, a Rule 61 hearing, an international arrest warrant, of which -- all of which he was aware from the very date of the original indictment in July of 1995, the circumstances of his surrender in May do not show that he would not be a flight risk in released. In fact, all of the evidence taken together, the circumstances of his surrender which were, in fact, compelled and the circumstances of his flight beforehand would show that he would be a flight risk and could not be relied upon to return to the Tribunal if he were released. I would draw to the Court's attention the decision in the Mrksic case on provisional release which was rendered after our filing on 24 July, 2002. That decision addressed some of these very issues. Some of the circumstances, the factual circumstances of that case, are similar to the circumstances in this case, though I would submit that the grounds for detention are much more compelling, much stronger, in that case than in the Mrksic case. In the Mrksic case, the Trial Chamber concerned the circumstances of a so-called voluntary surrender, which were quite similar to this accused's surrender, and found, in fact, it could not be considered voluntary and could not weigh very heavily in favour of release. And I would draw the Court's attention in particular to paragraphs 42 and 43 of that decision. In addition in that decision, the -- the Court discounted very heavily the accused's own personal guarantee that he would submit to the jurisdiction of the Court and would return for trial. A personal -- a similar personal guarantee has been offered in this case. The Court in Mrksic found in paragraph 45 of its decision that given the record of six years of flight, this personal guarantee from the accused was not very weighty and could not be considered as a very strong argument in favour of release. The second point I would make, and this is a -- this is, I think, a factual distinction from the Mrksic case and which makes this case, as I said, even more compelling, is that this accused was not just a fugitive for seven years but was what I would call an active fugitive. That is, he actively hid from an indictment of which he was aware, there is no doubt, and did so living under an alias, in hiding both in the RS and then later in Serbia. This is a significant point, I think, for two reasons. The first is it shows this accused's propensity to flee and to avoid the jurisdiction of this court and to avoid the Tribunal. But secondly, and as critically, it shows that this accused has had experience living on the run, living as a fugitive, and that experience is important because that's not an easy thing to do, living as a fugitive, and having that experience is something that he will be able to draw upon again if he is released flees again. The third point I would make is the accused has shown and we have attached Articles to our submission which I won't go through in length, but the accused has shown utter and repeated disdain for this court and for this indictment. And this goes back to the Jokic decision which this Chamber rendered, the decision on provisional release, which this Court outlined some of the considerations that should be taken into -- some of the factors that should be considered in considering provisional release. And in paragraph 23 of that decision, this Chamber said that because the Tribunal does not have its own arrest powers and is dependent on states for enforcing its powers, one thing that may be -- have to be considered is stringent conditions of release as a kind of substitute for the Tribunal's own -- the absence of powers by the Tribunal. In this case, the Prosecution would submit that there are no conditions of release that however stringent this court could reply upon, because in light of the utter disdain that this accused has shown for this Tribunal, for this Tribunal's orders, for its indictments, for its arrest warrant, and his repeated statements about this Tribunal, this Court could not have any confidence that this accused would abide by any conditions of release, would feel compelled either to appear or to abide by conditions of release however stringent. Therefore, we would submit that the conditions of release in this case cannot act as a substitute for a finding that this accused is not a flight risk, a finding which given all the evidence I don't think is available based on all the evidence. The next point is that the incentive -- the accused's incentive to flee is now greater than when he came to this Tribunal in May. In May, he obviously, as I said, made a calculation based on the circumstances at that time that it was in his best interest to surrender. He thought he was going to be arrested, and he wanted to get the guarantee from the government. Now the circumstances have changed. The Prosecution, as promised in its submission in July, has submitted an amended indictment for the Court's consideration which greatly expands the charges against this accused. The consequence of that is that this accused is facing -- now facing a greater likelihood of conviction, and he is also facing a greater likelihood of a longer sentence, which obviously will bear on his incentive and his calculation about whether he will flee or not. In addition, there are other circumstances that have changed. In May when he came to interest Tribunal, he was faced with this new law that had just been passed and the threat of immediate arrests. Well, in fact, there has just been one arrest under the new law. There have been a certain number of surrenders, but there are many individuals who have not been arrested. Therefore, if released, this accused could very well make a very different calculation about what his self-interest is, a calculation that would be similar to the calculation he made for seven years when he was living as a fugitive, a calculation that now -- that he's not likely to be arrested and now that he is facing a more serious indictment, it is in his interest to flee. Finally, I would address a few of the points that were made by Mr. Kastratovic. He stated that from the very beginning, his client has stated that he has trust in the Tribunal. Well, in fact, that representation is belied by the attachments to our submission which show that for years this accused has, as I said, shown disdain for this Tribunal, and only when he was forced to surrender did he begin making other kinds of statements. Mr. Kastratovic also represented that his client is seriously ill. Obviously that is a matter we are hearing about for the first time today, and I would submit is -- it is at this time not a factor that could be considered but would need to be dealt with in a more orderly fashion and a submission from Mr. Kastratovic with the relevant materials that we would have an opportunity to review. Mr. Kastratovic also submitted that Serbia and the federal government are not getting sufficient credit for their cooperation. It is true that there is a guarantee that has been submitted in this case. However, as we stated in our reply, that -- those guarantees, number one, should be treated with caution given the failure to arrest more fugitives that are -- that should be arrested, more fugitives from this Tribunal; and secondly - and I think an equally important point - the guarantees cannot, once again, be a substitute for a finding that has to be made under Rule 65(B) based on evidence that this accused is not a flight risk. He has the burden of showing through evidence that he is not a flight risk, and all the evidence, we would submit, is to the contrary and shows that, in fact, he is a flight risk. Finally, Your Honours, Mr. Kastratovic offered a -- offered on behalf of his client to grant an interview with the Prosecution. That is, of course, something that we would be interested in talking with Mr. Kastratovic further about, however, should have no bearing on his provisional release at this stage, should only -- could only possibly have a bearing on his release at a future time if, number one, the interview actually occurs; and number two, what occurs in the interview is that it is a truthful and complete interview by our judgement. Therefore, that is also a matter which at this stage, I would submit, should not weigh on whether this accused should obtain provisional release. If I could just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Nothing further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I may turn to the distinguished representative from the federal republic of Yugoslavia, his excellency Mr. Markovic, the Minister of Justice. You have the floor, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecution, the attorneys for the Defence, I have been authorised on behalf of the federal government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the government of the Republic of Serbia to offer guarantees for the accused, Mr. Milan Martic, in order for him to be provisionally released until the start of his trial. Since you have the text of the guarantees, there is no need for me to mention the items from that guarantee in particular or to go into any kind of detailed analysis of them, but I can state that these are serious guarantees of a serious state regardless of what the Prosecution thinks about that. Your Honour, Mr. Presiding Judge and Your Honours, my presence here today is the best test that my country, my state, and my people are seriously devoted to or committed to cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. That this is so, I would like to note that we only need to look at a few years back and to see how large a step forward we have made over the past year, because the former government not only did not cooperate with The Hague Tribunal but ignored the Tribunal. But since the democratic changes and the democratic government which came into power in the October events in 2001, you can see that this attitude has now changed and that we are committed to cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. Speaking about this is also the law that was adopted in the federal assembly and not in the assembly of Serbia. And they have also offered these guarantees. We have provided guarantees for several of the accused so far, and to date the guarantee in the case of Mr. Gruban has been positively resolved to date. What does a positive decision mean in this specific case? For us, it means a lot. There are a thousand and one reasons for us to ask you to decide positively on this matter, and I will only note the most important one. With a positive decision, we would strengthen the further cooperation of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with the International Criminal Tribunal. The public opinion, which is not a meaningless factor in any politically serious state. The faith would be strengthened that this Tribunal is not in the business of issuing selective justice but that it passes down true, real justice. The faith in the Tribunal would be strengthened, and it would, additionally, encourage some other people that are outside the reach of the law to voluntarily surrender for whom the federal state would offer its guarantees in turn. This would also strengthen the authority of the federal and the republican bodies of the government. In case of an unfavourable decision I am afraid that anti-democratic and retrograde forces would be directly encouraged, all the more so because we are approaching new elections in Serbia and Montenegro which form this joint state. A positive decision would have a very strong echo also in the international arena since we're on the brink of being accepted into the partnership for peace and the European Council. It would also indicate that we stick to our word. We have invited people to voluntarily surrender, and we have submitted guarantees and then it would be very negative if the Trial Chambers responded or decided negatively on the basis of these guarantees. That would demonstrate a certain attitude toward a state and its guarantees. I also am in favour of equal cooperation. Cooperation must go both ways because both partners in it are equal. If my country's a sovereign state, it should not just be something that is carrying out blindly the instructions of the Prosecution or the Tribunal. I'm almost finished, but I would just like to make a few more remarks about -- in response to what the Prosecution said. The Prosecutor said that the accused did not surrender voluntarily. According to our laws, the accused surrendered voluntarily, and I'm not going to speculate about this. With our guarantees, we guarantee that he will be accessible Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to the bodies, and we do not guarantee any kind of escape with these guarantees and any kind of thinking is not logical in this sense. The federal law has been adopt. The Prosecution is aware of this, and we believe that conditions have been created now for this matter to be positively resolved. Mr. Martic, even if he wanted to, and he does not want to, would have no place to flee. And once again, I thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kastratovic, you have something to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. S. KASTRATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you permit me just to response -- to respond to what the Prosecutor said. The Prosecutor, first of all, has a large quantity of contradictory statements that I am not able to comment on each one of those things. His excellency the Minister from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has said that the federal government has adopted this law on the 20th of April, 2002 -- yes, the year 2002. This Tribunal has -- Mr. Martic reported to this Tribunal on the 15th of May. So 25 days from the day of the adoption of this law. The second question which the Prosecution continuously insists on is flight. This Tribunal did not recognise the regime of Mr. Milosevic; this is a fact. There is a new regime as of October the 5th, and this is recognised, and it seeks cooperation. It has opened up its archives and wishes to cooperate fully. It wishes also to preserve the civil rights of its citizens. The Prosecution also talked about that. I never said that Martic recognised this court right from the beginning; I said quite the opposite. Martic did not recognise this court to the extent that this regime was not recognised by the Tribunal. But at this point, a new law has been adopted and he has acted in accordance with this law. And it says that a person who voluntarily surrenders to the Tribunal, the federal and republican government will offer guarantees for that person. So we have a very clear situation here, the situation in which the Prosecutor states that I stated that Mr. Martic is sick, well, I think it's quite the opposite. Perhaps they didn't quite understand me. I just wanted to state a metaphor, and I wanted to inform you that Mr. Martic, luckily is quite healthy, and that this ephemeral, unimportant fact of his unstable sugar levels, which is perhaps the case with many of us, is not reason why we are calling for or using as the reason to provisionally release him. I was just talking about something else, in fact, that the occasional accused should be returned on the basis of these guarantees, even if they are not in a serious health situation. As opposed to the situation with General Mrksic, no case, no accused has the same circumstances, personal or family circumstances, and their legal and factual circumstances are not the same. So the Prosecution of The Hague Tribunal cannot treat all the accused in a uniform way and to mummify its indictments. Also, the Prosecutor's remark about the fact that the amended -- about the amended indictment, it seems to us that this is not okay to include new charges. This indictment has been accepted. We will speak about this later, but this indictment does not practically exist. Why would we use that in our discussions here today when it practically does not exist? Their proposals regarding the indictment have not yet been dealt by the Chamber. So by talking about this, they're just prejudicing the accused, the interests of my government, and generally justice, which we expect from you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this Trial Chamber also received a motion filed by the accused himself -- excuse me. The request of provisional release until the beginning of trial. Mr. Martic, do you want to address on this subject to this Trial Chamber? If so, you may.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say a few words. First of all, I would like to thank my Federal Minister, Mr. Markovic, and also the representative of the embassy, Mr. Vukaskinovic, for finding time to come and provide these guarantees. I do not ask for mercy from this Tribunal. I expect justice. The remarks by the Prosecutor about possible flight or non-recognition of the court are, to a certain extent, true. I really did not recognise this court, and I had my reasons for that. The indictment which was issued against me expressly in 15 days for the bombardment of Zagreb, which I admit to, for reason that I hope will be understood why I did this. At the same time, no indictment was issued against the Croatian government and the politicians for the ethnic cleansing of my people. I did not recognise the court for these reasons. And second, nobody was backing me. I did not have a state. I came to Serbia when the law was adopted. Had anybody even backed me, I would have voluntarily surrendered. And the Prosecutor thinks that I did not want to come here. Couldn't I have stayed hidden away for a long time without anybody ever finding me? But I did not think that was the proper course of action. I decided to come in order to clear my name, first of all. And what is most important of all is in order for us to prove the truth about Krajina and to see who caused such an exodus of my people. The new indictment which I received is different from the first indictment. I would call it a packet of nebulous things which I believe that we will be able to reject with the help of my Defence counsel. So I would like to underscore the following amendment asking for mercy. Why would I need to be provisionally released? So that I could spend time in the summer house of my friend where I could prepare for my defence in peace with my attorneys, and then I would be able to be completely prepared to come to this trial in order to reject this package of nebulous matters. There is no need for me to hide. I have a state now, and I have asked God to give me somebody who could be able to give me support, and I have my country now. And I have no intention of escaping. If you believe that you should not grant this request for provisional release, that is up to you, but I do not wish to be here for two years waiting for some trial. And when this trial comes, I hope that it will be a true, just trial. If you release me, there is no need for me to repeat what my attorney and what the Minister stated. I will be reporting to the police. There are no reasons for me to flee. I have provided my telephone number, and if necessary, I can report daily to the police and to authorities of the Tribunal. But for principled reasons, it is important for me to show the truth about Krajina. I expect this to be a Tribunal that passes down justice, that hands down justice, and not the other thing which I do not wish to mention. That is all I wish to say. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. Well, I have some questions to ask. Mr. Kastratovic, you mentioned the conditions of your client, and you gave some explanations on that. I understand that this is a subject in the Status Conference, but since you have already mentioned it, would you please clarify your position on this issue? I mean the health conditions of your client. Are there any medical reports in this aspect, whether your client has been taken care of in the Detention Unit here?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. KASTRATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, Mr. Presiding Judge. Just like my client, I am not referring or using his health situation in this matter. His state of health is good. He's a man of 48 years, old, quite fit. He exercises, reads, and so on in the Detention Unit. I didn't even talk about that. I just wanted to talk about what the Prosecutor said through a metaphor, through a story. I wanted to state following: Do we need to wait for him to get sick so that we can release him so that he can die at home? This is what I was talking about. But he is a perfectly healthy man, and he has just stated that. I mentioned his sugar levels, blood sugar levels, but I you don't think you need to be offered any kind of proof regarding this matter because this is not something that should be taken into account while you are reaching your decision about granting or not granting the request for provisional release. His circumstances, his family circumstances --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. KASTRATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You asked me about -- you asked me about his personal family circumstances. I only talked about his family. Is this what you're asking, where he will be? I didn't quite understand what you were thinking of. If that's all, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think you have answered my question. Thank you very much. Any questions from other Judges? Judge El Mahdi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] I would like, if you allow me, to address the Defence counsel. If I understood him well, Mr. Martic decided to surrender the moment when the law was enacted, and I mean the law on the cooperation between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Tribunal. So if I understand well, he was aware of the indictment long before the date when he actually surrendered. Could the Defence please tell us at least approximately the day when he was informed, when he became aware of the indictment? And that's my first question. Second, very briefly, he mentioned using a pseudonym and a place of residence that he had chosen during the period between the date when he became aware of the indictment and the date when he surrendered voluntarily. How was it possible for him to take a pseudonym and live in hiding for six or seven years? Was it with the knowledge of the authorities or was it unknown to the authorities at the time? And that's my second question.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. KASTRATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first question -- my response to your first question is not going to be difficult when he decided to surrender. I would like to tell you something here. You never should forget that we were living in an autocratic regime of a man who is before -- who has been brought to trial before this Tribunal here today. I am not entering into any kind of details regarding that person. I do not wish him any -- anything ill. But Mr. Martic [as interpreted] did not recognise -- that person did not recognise the -- the international community or the Tribunal to which the bombing attests.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction not Mr. Martic but this other person.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. KASTRATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So under those circumstances, Mr. Martic did not have the opportunity to act, and he remained in the country. And at that point, as he had said himself, he did not have anybody to back him up in order for him to come forward. He should have been reported in 1995. Your Honours, do not forget that the Croatian state condemned Mr. Martic in absentia to a sentence of 99 years imprisonment. So do you really believe that he was fleeing only from The Hague Tribunal? He was fleeing from the Croatian authorities so that he would not arrest him and bring him before their courts. So in such a situation you cannot ask of a man who felt threatened end from several sides to think clearly and sensibly. The moment on the 5th of October, 2000, when the regime in Belgrade changed and when the authorities adopted the law that his excellency the Minister talked about, Mr. Martic surrendered himself 25 days after the adoption of this law. So these are the reasons that we are using to explain why he was in hiding and who he obtained these documents from, as you said, false documents, which we're not disputing. We are saying that he received those documents from the police of that regime. So I'm just explaining to you that in this situation, you need to be aware of the full circumstances of Mr. Martic's position. Not only from the aspect of the jurisdiction of this Tribunal but also from the aspect of the court -- decisions of the courts in Croatia which had sentenced him to almost 100 years' imprisonment. Who would not, I ask you, Your Honours, act in the same way? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge Orie, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've got a few questions for you, Mr. Kastratovic, or to be answered by the -- by Mr. Martic himself. Could you please tell me when exactly Mr. Martic was convicted in Croatia in absentia? What date? What year? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. KASTRATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not exactly, Your Honours. Mr. Martic was not condemned in one court. He was condemned in many courts in Croatia. From the year 1990, the bombing of Zagreb onwards, on many occasions the State of Croatia tried Mr. Martic. We even [as interpreted] received some of those judgements.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. We never received any of these judgements.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. KASTRATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there is no question that they exist. You can obtain them from the Croatian authorities and the Croatian courts, and I assure you that I'm not making it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kastratovic, if you make an argument that Mr. Martic was convicted and sentenced to a 99-year sentence, then it's up to you not to say that we can find these judgements but to tell this Chamber when, for example, the first of these judgements has been passed by what court. That's just providing us with the facts underlying your argument. Do you have this information?

utterances.speaker: MR. S. KASTRATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must remind you that I am aware that I have to prove my every claim. What I have been telling you about I know from the mass media. After the civil war in Yugoslavia, the relationship between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Croatia has deteriorated so much that I cannot even ask to get those judgements. All I can do is read about that in their press, in the Croatian press. And indeed I read in the Croatian press that Mr. Martic was condemned in absentia to 99 years. Perhaps it is not an exact figure. But if you displayed an interest and contacted the Croatian authorities, I am sure that you would be able to obtain these judgements. Mr. Martic probably knows more about this than I know, but I have read more than once in the Croatian press about trials in absence of Mr. Martic and the judgements handed down. I hope I have explained why I cannot be of more assistance in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Martic, do you know when for the first time you were convicted and sentenced in a Croatian court for the shelling of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not only the shelling of Zagreb. I never got a single indictment, not even the indictment from your Tribunal. All I know about indictments I know from the press. Croatia selectively raised its indictments, and I was able to find out about them only from the press. Exactly how many years I was condemned to, I never found out. Unfortunately, they are still doing it. The majority of the people who have been ethnically cleansed for only one purpose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking for further statements. I did put a question to you, and the answer of the question is quite clear to me, that you only have information from the press and you have no precise date or year or month for your first conviction. Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know exactly. All I know is from the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kastratovic, you repeatedly said that -- or at least it has been said that due to the lack of support of a national government, Mr. Martic was not in a position to surrender himself. What exactly has been changed? What is the support, apart from guarantees in respect of a request for provisional release, that is given at this very moment by the state in which he lives and of which he has the nationality? What's the support? Could you please explain to me what difference is? Apart from the guarantees, of course. We heard about the guarantees, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. S. KASTRATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, Your Honour, perhaps I did not make myself quite clear the first time. There was a regime in Yugoslavia, which you are very well aware of it, and it is now a relic. It ceased to exist on the 5th of October, 2001. Yugoslavia entered a new era on that date. Taking into account and understanding the important changes and the return of Yugoslavia into the democratic community, Yugoslavia understands it has to meet all the standards and requirements for actually becoming a part of that international community. One of the steps in that direction was the law that Yugoslavia adopted on cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. When we speak about that law, we are not only referring to specific guarantees. Please do not forget, Your Honours, that the investigators of the OTP are present everywhere in Yugoslavia. All the archives are open to them, everyone is available to them for interviews. They have the right to read, tape, record. And Yugoslavia is extending them its full cooperation for the sake of those more important political aims. What I was saying is that this law encouraged indictees, people who have been indicted by the Office of the Prosecutor, to surrender rather than be brought here by force, in which case they would not be in a position to ask for provisional release. Speaking of my client, I'm basing my request on his personal circumstances and the situation explained by the Federal Minister of Justice. You cannot -- you should not underestimate the presence of the Federal Minister of Justice of Yugoslavia. His presence here signifies the readiness of the federal government to consistently apply the law that has been enacted. I think the Office of the Prosecutor should admit here themselves how well they are received in Belgrade and how full a cooperation they are receiving. They have access to all the archives and documents. The people that Mr. Martic belonged to no longer exists in Croatia. And I don't mean only the Serbian people, I mean also the Albanian, Muslim, Croatian, Serbian, and other people who have all gone through ten years of great suffering. I'm only saying one thing here. Mr. Martic was a representative of one Serbian enclave which counted about a million people. There are no Serbs there anymore. And for the last seven years, he has refrained from involvement in politics, although he could have been politically involved. He is here today, and he will be here again any time you for it. If he doesn't come of his own free will, we have enforcement powers and tools and regulations and means to bring him here in handcuffs. He knows that he will not be released before he receives his final judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kastratovic, the whole accent during this argument is upon the attitude of the federal government and of the Serbian government. Would you agree with me that the main issue is the attitude of the accused? And if that is a positive that, of course, the support given by the government would certainly assist to convince the Court that a provision release might be taken into consideration, but the only thing I heard until now is that Mr. Martic said that when there was a change of regime that would favour the cooperation with the ICTY, then I will cooperate as well, and up to that moment, it was impossible for me. At the same time, all the press clippings received contain rather strong wordings. Like, if someone arrests me -- I don't know whether he said it or not, but you have not commented on that, I would consider this to be a terrorist act and I would do whatever I have to do under these circumstances. Is there any personal change in attitude apart from referring to the government? Is there any change in attitude between what he said before, according to these press clippings, since it's not easy to detect at this moment if someone says, "Well, I'm forced to go now because my government changed. There's a different regime now so I've got no choice." Isn't there a personal attitude and would you agree with me the personal attitude is the very first step to be taken into consideration? I don't know whether you want to answer the question or whether Mr. Martic wants to answer to that question, but I'm still not a clear view on his personal attitude rather than support of the government, which seems to be apparent over the last period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. KASTRATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give the floor to my client later if you allow me. But his explicit personal attitude is evident in his whole conduct, in the fact that he had reported to his own government, to his own Minister, and to this Tribunal, to all the people who are designated to receive his surrender by law. He accepted to be arrested. On the 15th of May of this year, he said so in so many words, "I recognised the Tribunal. I recognised the new authorities." Before that time, a different authority, different governments, were in power. There was a different regime, which also had an impact on his personal attitude. He expressed his real convictions by coming here where he is now in detention. And he has said himself that he will continue to recognise and respect this Court. You cannot hold it against him that he did not surrender voluntarily at once. He is no different from many others in that respect. It is not only the guarantees of the state that corroborate our motion for provisional release. There are other circumstances that you have to take into account; the expulsion of his people, their misfortune, the political regime that was in power before, his own circumstances. You must understand that these circumstances taken together had put him in the position in which he was. Once the regime in Yugoslavia changed, he surrendered immediately. I apologise to the interpreters. In this situation which I am trying to explain to you in greater detail, I believe it would perhaps be better for my client to say a few words about this if you are not pleased with my answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will perhaps be repeating myself, but let me say this once again. After the ethnic cleansing of the people whose president I was, I had no state. I was an apatriot, a man without a homeland. I was supposed to be extradited to the Tribunal as a citizen of Croatia. After all the things that I read in the Croatian press about my being condemned for this and that, the main point in all this writing, that our nation was not going to be allowed to return to that state, and I wanted to come here as a Yugoslav citizen. So I waited to get my Yugoslav passport, and as soon as I did, I came here. I reported not 25, as my counsel said, days after the enactment of the law. I reported after five days. But certain preparations had to be made before I came here. I am not asking for mercy. I'm asking for justice. And I want the truth about what is going on in my land of Krajina to finally come out from this Tribunal. That is my hope and my expectation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I put one question to the Prosecution. You have stressed again and again that the accused is still at risk of absconding. Do you have an explanation, apart from the proposed amended indictment, do you have an explanation why he did not flee when he was under the arrest -- under the threat of being arrested after the adoption of the domestic law? I mean, that would be the situation where there might be a need, if you want to abscond from justice, to act. Why do you expect him to -- to find a refuge somewhere else where he did not do that in the spring of this year?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, clearly in the spring of this year, when faced with the law on cooperation, the accused then made a calculation that it was in his interest to surrender. And we can't be exactly sure what went into that calculation, but the evidence would suggest that the calculation, after seven years of absconding, was based on a fear of immediate arrest, combined with an interest in obtaining the guarantees of the state which he could only do if he surrendered. So a calculation that was both fear of immediate arrest and also wanting to obtain provisional release. Why would it be different in the future? We submit that this calculation could change and is likely to change at any time because the circumstances that will enter into the calculation will change. The first circumstance that was cited by the Court itself, that is the amendment has been changed. So now the calculation is different because the indictment is expanded and it's a more serious indictment. That changes the calculation. Also now, there is a bit of a track record with respect to the law on cooperation. When the accused surrendered in May, at that time he could have expected that all of the fugitives would be immediately arrested. Well, that, in fact, has not happened. In fact, there has openly been one arrest. There are a number of outstanding fugitives, and in fact, some rather prominent visible fugitives in Serbia who have not been arrested. Based on that, the calculation could be different. This Court, we would submit, cannot rely on the calculation always being the same every single day if this accused were released. In fact, based on the circumstances of his surrender, what actually made him surrender? The unique circumstances and his past conduct and past unwillingness to come to this Tribunal when nothing prevented him from doing so would suggest that it is very likely that a day will come and he will, of course on provisional release, have some time to prepare this, but a day will come when he will abscond and seek refuge either in his own country under -- again under an alias or perhaps in another country and that he would gain through provisional release the time to be able to implement that. If I may, there was an earlier question about when this accused knew, was aware, of this indictment, and I would draw the Court's attention to page 1 of our appendix to our filing in July which is an article from the 26th of July, 1995, the day after the indictment -- the first indictment against him was confirmed in which the accused is quoted speaking about the indictment. Presumably he was well aware of it the day after the indictment on the 26th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one other short question to you. You said, as far as I remember, that the burden of proof to demonstrate that there is no risk of fleeing would be on the shoulders of the accused. What is exactly the legal basis for that assertion?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was relying on this Court's judgement Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in the Jokic case in which that was the conclusion after reviewing the law of this court. And the Jokic order is from the 27th of February, 2002. I draw the Court's attention to paragraph 17 in which it comes to that conclusion. I believe that every other Trial Chamber that has considered that issue with the exception of a dissent from Judge Robinson in one matter, has reached the same conclusion. I would also note that in the Brdjanin provisional release decision of 25 July, 2000, in paragraphs 16 and 22, that Trial Chamber found that not only was this burden on the accused but found that it is also a substantial burden on the accused. I would also make one final point and that is that the Prosecution is also -- also submits that the evidence would suggest that this accused poses a danger to victims, witnesses, or other persons, which is the second part of 65(B), Rule 65(B). That has not been addressed but it is our argument based on the evidence that we stand by here as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think that's all for today's hearing on the provisional release of Mr. Martic. Yes, Mr. Kastratovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. KASTRATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not respond to what the Prosecutor said, because he has made some lump sum judgements, as if we were trading on the market. He is trying to guess at what is going on in Mr. Martic's head. He can get it into his head he wants to commit suicide and do it, or something else may happen. He may get a terminal illness and die. We cannot know what will happen in the future. There is another thing that we must take into account and that is possible danger to victims. And that is why I mentioned all the things I mentioned about Mr. Martic. He cannot leave the country even if he wanted to abscond, precisely because all the victims and all the witnesses are in Croatia, not in Serbia. He is bound by his situation. He is between a rock and a hard place. He can be arrested by two sides. He is tied to the place where he resides. So any suggestions about his being a flight risk are groundless, in my view. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this Trial Chamber will deliberate this issue, taking into account the submissions by both parties as well as the guarantees submitted by the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. We will make our decisions at a later stage. Now we will have a short break. Then at ten minutes to 1, we will resume our Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Hearing adjourned at 12.28 p.m., to be followed by a Status Conference
